rationale: Studies differ a lot in sequencing depth, 16S region and protocol, so the same genus can sit at very different abundance levels in each study. I will standardize log relative abundance within each study (z-score per genus per study, no labels used) before the random forest. Then its splits follow how a genus differs from its own study's typical level, not how studies differ from each other.

IBD is known for lower gut microbial diversity, and a random forest that only sees per-genus z-scores cannot easily rebuild community-wide diversity from them. This change adds alpha-diversity features at OTU and genus level: Shannon, inverse Simpson, and depth-controlled Hurlbert rarefied richness. Hurlbert richness is exact and deterministic. All three are z-scored within study, like the genus features, so depth and protocol differences between studies are removed.

Every OTU without a named genus currently goes into a single `g__` bucket, so signal from unnamed genera in different families gets mixed together. That bucket includes many unclassified Ruminococcaceae, Lachnospiraceae and Enterobacteriaceae OTUs, which are central to IBD. This change adds family-level and phylum-level log relative abundances, z-scored within study like the other features. The forest can then use the well-known IBD shifts at family and phylum level: loss of Ruminococcaceae and Lachnospiraceae, and gain of Enterobacteriaceae and Proteobacteria. These higher levels should also be more consistent across studies than genus labels.

Many genera and families are present in only a few samples, so after within-study z-scoring they are mostly noise. With a √p feature sample at each split, these rare columns push informative ones out of the candidate set. This change drops any taxon whose prevalence is below 10% in every study (label-free filtering). The forest should then split more often on well-supported IBD taxa, and the change still keeps taxa that only one study detects.

I'm adding an L2-regularized logistic regression on the same study-standardized features and averaging its ranks with the random forest. The penalty strength is picked by inner grouped CV on `ctx["groups_train"]`, scored by AUROC. IBD dysbiosis is mostly a broad, additive shift (loss of many Firmicutes taxa, gain of Proteobacteria, lower diversity), which a linear model on z-scored log abundances captures smoothly. The forest captures threshold effects and interactions, so their errors should differ and the blend should rank samples better than either alone.

Many IBD studies describe dysbiosis as a sample sitting far from the healthy community, with patients scattered in many directions (the "Anna Karenina" pattern). A linear model on single taxa can't see that kind of spread. Inside `fit_predict` I add three features for each sample: its distance to the training-control centroid of its own study, its distance to the training-case centroid, and the difference between the two. The centroids are built from the study-standardized taxon profiles, and each training sample is left out of its own class centroid so the features don't leak its label. Study is used only to decide which centroid a sample is compared with, not as a predictor.

Every OTU with no genus name currently lands in one shared `g__` column, so unclassified Ruminococcaceae, Lachnospiraceae and Enterobacteriaceae OTUs all mix together. Those groups move in opposite directions in IBD and carry a large share of reads. I'll key each unnamed OTU by its deepest named rank instead (e.g. `f__Ruminococcaceae;g__`), which gives separate abundance features that can be compared across studies.

Within-study z-scoring centres each feature on that study's own case/control mix, so the same score means different things in studies with different case ratios. This change follows Gibbons/Duvallet/Alm's (2018) percentile normalization: inside `fit_predict`, each sample's features become percentiles of the training-control distribution of its own study, mapped to normal scores, for both train and test. Controls then sit at a shared "healthy" reference in every study, and cases are scored by how far they move from it. Only training labels are used, and the mapping is monotone within each study.

Adding family and phylum levels gave the largest gain so far (+0.033). This round adds the two ranks in between, class and order, as log relative abundances z-scored within study. Several of the most consistent IBD shifts sit at these ranks: more Gammaproteobacteria/Enterobacteriales, fewer Clostridia/Clostridiales, and changes in Bacilli and Erysipelotrichi. These ranks also pool reads that have no genus or family assignment, so they should be more stable across studies than the finer levels.

I'm adding a shallow, strongly regularized LightGBM classifier as a third member of the rank-average ensemble. It uses the same study-standardized multi-level features. A boosted model fits the residuals the forest leaves behind, so it can pick up threshold and interaction effects that differ from the forest's. These include the joint loss of butyrate producers together with a Proteobacteria bloom, which bagged forests and the linear model each capture only partly. Its errors should therefore differ from the other two models, and the blend should rank samples better.

I'm adding the Gevers 2014 microbial dysbiosis index as a label-free known-marker feature. It is the log ratio of the IBD-enriched families (Enterobacteriaceae, Pasteurellaceae, Veillonellaceae, Fusobacteriaceae, Neisseriaceae, Gemellaceae) to the depleted taxa (Bacteroidales, Clostridiales, Erysipelotrichaceae, Bifidobacteriaceae), plus the summed abundance of each side, all z-scored within study. Each single taxon is noisy, but this index collapses the published IBD shift into one stable, ratio-based axis that is less affected by study depth or composition. The forest, booster and logistic regression can all use it directly.

Within-study z-scoring centres each feature on that study's own case/control mix, and the four studies have very different case ratios. So the pooled models partly learn which study-level class balance a z-score came from rather than the dysbiosis itself. This change gives training samples sample weights (only training labels and study are used) so that cases and controls carry equal total weight inside each study, while each study keeps its overall weight. All three models (forest, logistic regression, booster) then learn the case-vs-control contrast within each study, which is exactly what the within-study AUROC scores.

All abundance features currently use a fixed pseudocount, log10(rel + 1e-5). In shallow samples a single read (or one fewer) moves a taxon by about 1.5 log units, so sampling noise near the detection limit becomes a large share of each within-study z-score. I'm switching every level to a count-scale pseudocount, log10((count + 0.5) / total), the usual half-read zero replacement in compositional analysis. Each zero then sits just below that sample's own detection limit, and singletons count for less (about 0.5 log units). This should give the forest, the logistic regression and the booster a cleaner abundance signal and shrink the depth-driven differences between studies. This is a proposal only; I haven't run it, so there is no Dev score yet.

I'm adding a CatBoost classifier as a fourth member of the rank average. Its symmetric (oblivious) depth-4 trees and ordered boosting are strongly regularized, which suits a few-thousand-sample, noisy, study-standardized feature set. Its errors should differ from those of the leaf-wise LightGBM, the bagged random forest and the linear model, so the blended ranking should be more stable. Adding complementary ensemble members has given the gains in rounds 5 and 10.

IBD involves a loss of whole taxa, not just lower abundance, but a zero in the log-abundance features depends on each sample's sequencing depth, which varies widely both within and between studies. I'll add the exact rarefied detection probability for each named genus at 2,000 reads, the per-genus version of the Hurlbert richness we already use. It is deterministic, uses no labels, keeps only genera present in at least 5% of samples overall, and is z-scored within study. This gives the models a depth-controlled presence/absence signal that log abundance captures only partly.

IBD dysbiosis is a coordinated loss or gain of whole guilds, such as butyrate-producing Clostridiales and facultative-anaerobe blooms, while single-genus abundances are noisy. This change adds label-free co-abundance groups: named genera present in at least 10% of samples are clustered by the correlation of their within-study z-scores (average linkage, cut at 1−r = 0.7). Each group of three or more genera becomes one feature, the mean of its members' z-scores, re-standardized within study. This should give all three models denoised guild-level axes that hold up better across studies.

Within-study AUROC only depends on how samples are ordered inside each study, but the current ensemble converts each model's scores to ranks over the whole pooled test fold. If one model's scores shift between studies, those pooled ranks squeeze its spread within a study, and the blend gives that model less weight than intended. This change converts each model's predictions to percentile ranks within each test study (using `meta_test` study only for grouping, never as a predictor) before averaging, so all three models get equal weight on the ranking that is actually scored. I haven't run it, so there is no Dev score yet.

I'm replacing the random forest with an ExtraTrees classifier (1000 trees, min_samples_leaf=2). After within-study z-scoring, many taxa have zero-heavy, study-specific distributions. A random forest's greedy best-cut thresholds can lock onto noise and study-specific cut points, while randomized thresholds average over many cut points. That should give smoother, better-calibrated rankings that hold across the four studies. I haven't run this, so there is no Dev score yet.

I'm replacing the per-study mean/SD z-score with a per-study rank-based inverse-normal transform (Blom scores, ties averaged). It uses no labels and maps every feature to the same distribution inside each study. The log abundances are zero-inflated and skewed, and the shape of that skew depends on the study's depth and 16S region. Matching only the mean and SD therefore leaves thresholds and LR coefficients misaligned across the four studies. Matching the whole distribution should line them up better, and it also limits the pull of outliers on the logistic regression. I haven't run this, so there is no Dev score yet.

The IBD signal sits in a fairly small set of taxa and diversity axes, such as Enterobacteriaceae, Faecalibacterium, Roseburia and Ruminococcaceae. The pure-L2 logistic regression spreads weight over hundreds of noisy rare-taxon columns, so I'm replacing it with an elastic-net logistic regression. Inner grouped CV, scored by AUROC, picks both C and the L1 ratio. The grid includes an L1 ratio of 0, so the current L2 model stays available if sparsity doesn't help.
